22.title: The boy at the door
22.hook: Parvati makes a son from earth; sets him to guard her bath
22.howItsDone: Some Hindu families keep an image of Ganesha by the front door or at the entrance of a shop, as the guardian of thresholds, and his birth story is often retold at Ganesh Chaturthi.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gita: a conversation in a chariot, and the line, you have the right to act, not to the fruit. Today, the stories begin, and the first one starts in a bathroom.
screen: `YOU HAVE THE RIGHT TO ACT. NOT TO THE FRUIT.`

segments.voice: A goddess wants to take a bath in peace. That's the whole problem. Parvati lives with Shiva on Mount Kailash, and the door is guarded by his ganas, his attendants, loyal to him. Whenever Shiva wants to walk in, they step aside. Nobody in the house is simply hers. So she takes the paste she rubbed on her skin before bathing, the dust of her own body, and shapes it into a boy. She breathes life into him, and the first face he ever sees is his mother's. She hands him a staff: guard this door. Let no one in. No one at all. He has only just opened his eyes, and already he has a job. That boy grows up to be Ganesha.
screen: `A GODDESS WANTS A BATH.` → `NOBODY IS HERS.` → `A BOY FROM EARTH.` → `GUARD THIS DOOR.`

segments.voice: You met Ganesha on day one, as a word. Now, his story. This telling comes from the Shiva Purana, a collection of stories about Shiva, and it isn't the only version. Look where he comes from: not a birth, but what his mother washed from her own skin, the ordinary stuff of a bath. The god of beginnings begins as earth, shaped by hands. And look why. Parvati isn't lonely. She needs someone at the door. In a house full of servants loyal to someone else, she wants one person whose whole job is to protect her space. Some things need a guard. A bath. A conversation. A quiet morning before the phone wakes up. The boy is new. He knows nothing about who lives here or who outranks whom. He knows one instruction, and he means to keep it. It fits that Ganesha images often hang by front doors: he's honored as the keeper of thresholds, where outside becomes inside. Tomorrow someone very large walks up to that door, sure it's his house too. And the boy says no.

segments.voice: Your first two-minute sit: picture a door, the door to a room that's just yours. When something knocks, a message, a worry, a replay of an argument, don't fight it; notice it, say kindly, not now, and let it wait outside. Each time something knocks, notice it, and go back to guarding, like the boy.
Ganas: Shiva's attendants, who guard his house. The boy made of earth will grow up to lead them. This is the start of his story.
Your line: some things need a guard. Parvati made hers out of earth. See you tomorrow.

23.title: Shiva comes home
23.hook: the fight; the head; Parvati's grief stops the universe
23.howItsDone: Hindus tell this story as part of Ganesha's birth, often at Ganesh Chaturthi, carrying both the weight of Parvati's grief and the mending that follows.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was ganas, Shiva's attendants, and Parvati made a boy from earth with one instruction: some things need a guard. Today, someone comes to the door.

Shiva has been away, and now he walks home up the mountain, to his own house. At his own door there's a boy he has never seen, holding a staff. The boy says: you can't come in. Shiva says: this is my house. The boy says: my mother said no one. Anyone. Shiva sends his ganas to move the child. The boy beats them back. More come. He beats them back too. The gods arrive to help, and in the Shiva Purana even they can't get past him. A house fight has turned into a war. And then Shiva, who has never been told no at his own door, raises his trident. And the boy's head is gone.
screen: `A STRANGER AT HIS OWN DOOR.` → `THE BOY SAYS NO.` → `THE TRIDENT.`

segments.voice: This is a hard story, and the tradition doesn't soften it. Both of them are right. The boy is keeping his word to his mother. Shiva is trying to walk into his own home. Nobody is the villain, and something terrible happens anyway. Family fights can look like that. Now Parvati comes out, and her grief is not quiet. In the Shiva Purana, she is so angry and so heartbroken that she calls up goddesses, fierce forms of her own power, and sends them to swallow the universe. Heaven starts to come apart. The gods who fought the boy now come begging. The sage Narada and the gods plead with her, and she gives them her terms: bring my son back to life, and give him a place of honor among you. Otherwise, no universe. Two things here. First: grief has power. This tradition doesn't tell a mother to calm down. Her grief stops everything, and everyone has to deal with it. Second: the one who broke it has to fix it. Shiva, the great god, has to mend what he broke, and he agrees. What broke can be mended. Not unbroken. The boy will not come back the same, and tomorrow you'll see how he comes back. But mended. Shiva is often honored as the one who destroys so that things can begin again. Here, he has to help something begin again.

segments.voice: Sit with something in your life that broke: a friendship, a promise, maybe something you broke yourself without meaning to, and look at it honestly, the way Parvati refused to pretend, without trying to fix it. Ask one question: could this be mended, not made new, but mended? If you pray, you can hold it up to God; if you don't, just hold it.
Trident, the weapon Shiva raised at his own door. The fight that followed, and Parvati's grief, strong enough that the gods agree to mend what they broke.
Your line: what broke can be mended. Parvati would not let it stay broken. Day twenty-three, done.

24.title: The elephant facing north
24.hook: the search; the head; the boy lives
24.howItsDone: Many Hindus begin weddings, housewarmings, new ventures and other ceremonies by honoring Ganesha first, often with a short prayer or mantra to him before anything else begins.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the trident: a boy lost his head at his mother's door, and her grief stopped the universe. What broke can be mended. Today, the mending.

Go north, Shiva tells his ganas. Bring back the head of the first living creature you meet. They run down off the mountain, into the forests, heading north. The first creature they find is an elephant; in the version most families tell, it's asleep with its head toward the north. They bring the head back. Shiva sets it on the boy's body and breathes life into him, and the boy opens his eyes for the second time in his life. His mother is there again. But now he has a trunk, wide ears, and a face every child in India can draw by the age of four.
screen: `GO NORTH.` → `THE FIRST CREATURE YOU MEET.` → `AN ELEPHANT.` → `HE OPENS HIS EYES AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Why an elephant? The story's plain answer: it was the first creature they met. But Hindus have long found meaning in that face. Big ears, to listen more than he speaks. A small mouth. A trunk that can uproot a tree or pick up a single grain of rice. An elephant doesn't go around the forest; it walks through and makes a path. That's the remover of obstacles you met on day one, and now you know where the face came from. The versions differ, and it's worth saying so. The tradition keeps them side by side. The Shiva Purana says north, the first creature. Popular tellings add the sleeping elephant. Another text, the Brahmavaivarta Purana, has the head lost for another reason entirely. Then the part that matters most. When the boy wakes, Shiva doesn't just forgive him; he honors him. He makes him leader of the ganas, the very guards who fought him. That's his name: Ganesha, Ganapati, lord of the ganas. And with all the gods listening, Shiva promises that this boy will be worshipped first, before any other god, before any ceremony. So to this day, a Hindu wedding, a housewarming, a new business, a first day of school often starts with Ganesha. First, before anyone. The boy who was killed at the door becomes the one who opens every door.

segments.voice: Think of something that broke and came back different, but whole: a friendship after a fight, a body after an injury, you after a hard year. Maybe it came back with a new face, like the boy. Thank it, or whoever helped mend it; some people say that thank-you to God.
Ganesha: the elephant-headed lord of the ganas, brought back to life and promised to be honored first.
Your line: first, before anyone. Shiva's promise to the boy at the door. That's day twenty-four.

screen: `DAY 24 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE RACE AROUND THE WORLD.`

25.title: The race around the world
25.hook: Ganesha vs Kartikeya: one circles the earth, one circles his parents
25.howItsDone: Hindus walk pradakshina, a clockwise circle keeping the holy on their right, around temple shrines, sacred trees and the wedding fire; this story is often told to children to explain why parents are honored.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ganesha: an elephant's head, a second waking, and a promise that he's honored first, before anyone. Today he gets a brother, and a race.

A peacock against a mouse. Two brothers: Kartikeya, the warrior, fast and bright, on his peacock, and Ganesha, round and patient, on his mouse. Their parents, Shiva and Parvati, set a contest: whoever goes around the whole world first, wins. Kartikeya doesn't wait for the end of the sentence. He's gone, over mountains, over oceans, around the entire earth. Ganesha looks at his mouse. The mouse looks at Ganesha. So Ganesha walks over to his mother and father and, slowly, carefully, walks a circle around them. He bows. And he says: I'm done.
screen: `A PEACOCK AND A MOUSE.` → `AROUND THE WHOLE WORLD.` → `HE CIRCLES HIS PARENTS.`

segments.voice: Kartikeya lands, out of breath, to find his brother already declared the winner. In the Shiva Purana's telling, Ganesha explains: the scriptures teach that walking around your parents with devotion is the same as walking around the whole earth. My world is right here, and I went around it. That walk is real. It's called pradakshina: circling something holy, keeping it on your right. Hindus do it at temples, around a shrine, a sacred tree, the fire at a wedding. It says: this is the center, and I move around it. So Ganesha isn't pulling a trick. He's doing what people do at a temple, and naming where his center is. The versions differ. In the Shiva Purana the prize is who gets married first, and Ganesha does. In a telling from South India it's a single fruit of wisdom, brought by the sage Narada. Kartikeya, called Murugan there, loses, leaves home and goes to live on a hill: Palani, in Tamil Nadu, home today to one of his great temples. Pilgrims still climb it. So the story has two winners, depending on who tells it. And Kartikeya isn't the fool. He really went around the world. Ganesha just noticed that the world he cared about was a few steps away. The whole world is close.
screen: `MY WORLD IS RIGHT HERE.` · `PRADAKSHINA — CIRCLING THE CENTER.` · `A WEDDING, OR A FRUIT.` · `KARTIKEYA ISN'T THE FOOL.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE WORLD IS CLOSE.`

segments.voice: If you can, stand and pick a center, a chair, a plant, a photo of someone you love, and walk slowly around it, keeping it on your right, one step per breath. As you walk, think of the few people who are your whole world. If you can't walk right now, trace a slow circle with one finger around their names.
Pradakshina: circling something holy, keeping it on your right. Kartikeya circled the earth; Ganesha circled his parents.
Your line: the whole world is close. Sometimes it's a few steps away. Until tomorrow.

26.title: The broken tusk
26.hook: the pen breaks mid-Mahabharata; he snaps his tusk to finish
26.howItsDone: Ganesha is honored as a patron of writing and learning; some Hindus write a line honoring him at the top of a new notebook or account book before they begin.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pradakshina: Ganesha circled his parents and called it the whole world. The whole world is close. Today, look closely at his face.

Count the tusks on a Ganesha statue. One is whole. The other is snapped short, and often he's holding the broken piece in his hand. The story behind it is a writer's story. The sage Vyasa has a vast poem in his head, the Mahabharata, and needs someone to write it down as he speaks. He asks Ganesha. Ganesha says yes, on one condition: once I start, you can't stop. If you pause, I leave. Vyasa adds one of his own: you can't write a single line until you understand it. They begin. Then, somewhere in the middle, Ganesha's pen breaks.
screen: `COUNT THE TUSKS.` → `A VAST POEM IN HIS HEAD.` → `DON'T STOP. UNDERSTAND.` → `THE PEN BREAKS.`

segments.voice: He can't stop; that was his own rule. So, the story goes, he snaps off his own tusk, dips it in the ink and keeps writing. That's why he's called Ekadanta, the one with one tusk. A word on sources. The scribe story is told at the beginning of the Mahabharata in some versions of the text; the modern critical edition leaves that passage out. The tusk as a pen is a later telling still, and other Puranas explain the broken tusk in different ways, including a fight with the warrior-sage Parashurama. The tradition keeps all of them, so hold it as a story, not a record. And look at what it holds. Two conditions: don't stop, and understand before you write. Tradition says Vyasa slipped in knotty verses to slow his scribe down and catch a breath. Speed and understanding, keeping each other honest. Then: the tool breaks, and the work doesn't. Ganesha gives up something of his own, something permanent, so the work gets finished. The remover of obstacles meets a broken pen, and the answer is himself. Half-finished things pile up: a letter, a course, a drawer. The story doesn't say it'll be easy. It says finish the thing, even if it costs you a tusk.

segments.voice: Let one small unfinished thing come to mind: an email half-written, a dish in the sink, a thank-you never sent. Picture yourself finishing it, start to end, and notice, without blame, what has been stopping you.
Ekadanta: the one-tusked, Ganesha's name after he snapped his own tusk to keep writing the Mahabharata without stopping.
Your line: finish the thing. The tool can break; the work doesn't have to. Twenty-six days in.

27.title: The mouse
27.hook: a mountain of a god rides a mouse
27.howItsDone: In Hindu temples and home shrines a god's vahana often sits facing the deity; at Ganesh Chaturthi Ganesha's mouse is placed at his feet, sometimes with its own small offering.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ekadanta: the tusk Ganesha snapped so the writing wouldn't stop. Finish the thing. Today, look down, at his feet.

Here's a picture that makes children laugh. Ganesha: big belly, elephant head, four arms, sitting like a king. And under him, carrying all of it, a tiny mouse, often looking up at him, sometimes nibbling a sweet. It makes no physical sense at all, and that's the point. In this tradition, gods have animals that carry them. Shiva rides Nandi, the bull. Vishnu rides Garuda, the great eagle. Durga rides a lion. Saraswati has her swan. Kartikeya, from the race, has his peacock. And the god of beginnings, the remover of obstacles, rides the smallest of them all.
screen: `A BIG GOD. A TINY MOUSE.` → `GODS HAVE THEIR RIDES.` → `THE SMALLEST OF ALL.`

segments.voice: The word is vahana, from a Sanskrit root, vah, to carry. A vahana is the one that carries: a vehicle, a mount. And it's more than transport; it tells you something about the god. People read the bull as strength and patience, the eagle as speed, the lion as courage. So why a mouse? Hindus give more than one answer. One: a mouse gets into everything, through walls, under doors, into the grain store. It finds a way in where nothing bigger could, which is what the remover of obstacles does. Two: the mouse is desire, restless, nibbling at everything, never satisfied. Ganesha doesn't kill it. He rides it, and steers it. Wanting doesn't go away; it just stops being in charge. Three, and simplest: the huge is carried by the small. Stories of where the mouse came from vary a lot. In some Puranas it's a being who was cursed, or a demon Ganesha defeated who became his mount, and no single one is the official answer. What they share is the picture. At Ganesh Chaturthi, the mouse sits at his feet in homes and street shrines, sometimes with its own little offering. And look at who's doing the lifting. Not the god. The mouse. Small carries large. Every day, quietly.

segments.voice: Look around you, or think back over today, and find one small thing holding up something large: the chair under you, one bolt in a bridge, the person at the front desk, a habit that keeps your week from falling apart. Pick one, look at it, and give it credit.
Vahana: the one that carries, the animal each god rides. Ganesha's is a mouse.
Your line: small carries large. Under the god, the little mouse does the lifting. Day twenty-seven, carried.

28.title: Modak
28.hook: why he's always eating; the sweet as a gift that returns
28.howItsDone: At temples and home shrines Hindus offer food to the deity and then share it as prasad; at Ganesh Chaturthi many families make modaks, offer them to Ganesha, and give them out to family and neighbors.

segments.voice: Yesterday, vahana: the mouse that carries a god. Small carries large. Today closes Ganesha's week, with the sweet in his hand.

A little dumpling of rice flour, pinched shut at the top like a flower bud, filled with coconut and jaggery. That's a modak, and in images of Ganesha there's often one in his hand, low, near that round belly. One of his names means the one who loves modaks, and at his festival, Ganesh Chaturthi, families make them by the trayful. People tell a story about his appetite. Kubera, a rich god proud of his wealth, invites Ganesha to a feast to show off. Ganesha eats every dish, every pot, and he's still hungry. Nothing Kubera owns can fill him.
screen: `A DUMPLING LIKE A FLOWER BUD.` → `THE ONE WHO LOVES MODAKS.` → `A FEAST THAT CAN'T FILL HIM.`

segments.voice: What finally satisfies him is something tiny: a handful of plain food, given with love. Not the feast. The love. The story isn't in one fixed text; it's the kind families pass down. But it points at something central to how Hindus worship with food. Today's word, prasad, means grace, a gift given freely. At a temple or a home shrine, food is offered to the god: sweets, fruit, rice. It sits before the image a while, then it's taken back and shared with everyone there. And now it's different. Not leftovers. Prasad: the same food, returned as a blessing. People often receive it with the right hand, or with both hands cupped, and try not to waste a crumb. So the offering comes back. You give, and what you gave is handed back to you, and you share it. Read that way, Ganesha's appetite isn't greed. He receives first, so that everyone else can receive after. Now look back at the week. A boy made of earth, guarding a door. A trident, and a mother's grief. An elephant's head, and a promise: first, before anyone. A race, and a small circle around the people who are your world. A broken tusk, and the thing finished. A mouse, carrying a mountain. And a sweet, handed back. Seven days with one god.

Prasad: grace. Food offered to God and handed back as a blessing, to be shared.
